694.title: Tisha B'Av: Lamentations
694.hook: read by candlelight, sitting low; the Talmud says the second Temple fell for baseless hatred (Yoma 9b)
694.howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations chanted in a dim synagogue, followed by kinot, poems of mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the fast that opens three weeks of mourning. Your line was walls breached. Did you find a crack that needs mending? Three weeks later, the fire. Day six hundred ninety-four.

Evening, in a synagogue, on the ninth of Av. The big lights are off or turned low. In many places the curtain has been taken down from the ark. People have come in sneakers or cloth shoes, because leather is set aside for the day. Nobody greets anyone. They don't sit on the benches; they sit on the floor, or on low stools, the way mourners sit at home. Someone has a candle, someone has a phone flashlight. And then a reader begins a slow, falling chant, and the first word is a cry.
screen: `THE LIGHTS GO LOW.` → `NO LEATHER, NO GREETINGS.` → `EVERYONE SITS ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: The word is eicha. It means how, the kind of how you say when you can't believe what you're seeing. It's the first word of the book of Lamentations, and Jews call the whole book by it. The old Jewish translation opens: How doth the city sit solitary. Jerusalem, once full of people, sits alone like a widow. The book has five chapters, and four of them are built on the alphabet, verse by verse, from the first letter to the last, as if grief needed every letter there is. Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, is the day the tradition remembers both Temples falling: the first to Babylon, the second to Rome, centuries apart, mourned on one day. It's a full fast, from sunset to the next nightfall. Now the question every mourner asks: why? The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, gives an answer that has stung for centuries. The first Temple, it says, fell because of idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed. But the second Temple? People then studied Torah, kept the commandments, and did acts of kindness. So why did it fall? Because of sinat chinam, baseless hatred. Hatred for nothing, for no reason worth the name. And the Talmud adds that baseless hatred weighs as much as those three great sins together. Notice what that does. The rabbis didn't only blame the empire with the battering rams. They looked at their own community: the feuds, the contempt, the neighbor nobody would speak to. And the book doesn't end in the dark. Its last chapter asks God to turn us back and renew our days as of old, and because the very last verse is so bitter, the congregation goes back and says that line again.
screen: `EICHA: HOW?` · `TWO TEMPLES, ONE DAY OF MOURNING.` · `NOT ONLY ROME: BASELESS HATRED.` · `SAY THE HOPEFUL LINE AGAIN.` · then, large: `BASELESS HATRED DESTROYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one grudge. If you can, sit low, on the floor or on a step. Let your breathing settle. Then let one grudge come to mind, the kind that isn't about anything big anymore: an old slight, a sibling's tone, a neighbor you decided long ago not to like. Look at what it's built on. Often, not much. You don't have to forgive the unforgivable, and you don't have to call anyone. Just, for this minute, set this one down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor. Notice your shoulders when it's gone. The bell holds the time.
Eicha. How: the first word and the Hebrew name of Lamentations, read on Tisha B'Av, sitting low. Today's word.
Your line: baseless hatred destroys. Today, catch one moment of contempt, in your head, online or out loud, and let it go unsaid. Day six hundred ninety-four.

fork.reveal: the Talmud (Yoma 9b) says baseless hatred, and that it weighs as much as idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed together.

695.title: Tu B'Av (Mishnah Taanit 4:8)
695.hook: six days after the saddest day comes a day of love, when young women danced in the vineyards
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the whole Torah
695.howItsDone: Tu B'Av, the fifteenth of Av, has no fixed rituals in Jewish law beyond omitting some penitential prayers; in modern Israel it is celebrated as a day of love, popular for weddings, parties and romance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eicha, Lamentations read sitting on the floor. Your line was baseless hatred destroys. Did you set one grudge down? Now count six days past the saddest day. Day six hundred ninety-five.

There were no happier days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur. That's the claim, near the end of a tractate of the Mishnah about fasts, in the name of a sage called Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Yom Kippur? The day of not eating, of confessing, of standing all day in white? Happy? And the fifteenth of Av, a date most people have never heard of, sitting just six days after the day Jerusalem is mourned on the floor. Today, the strangest happy day in the calendar.
screen: `NO HAPPIER DAYS THAN THESE.` → `YOM KIPPUR? HAPPY?` → `SIX DAYS AFTER THE SADDEST DAY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tu B'Av means the fifteenth of Av. Hebrew letters are numbers, and fifteen is written tet and vav, nine and six, which together sound like tu. Then the Mishnah tells us what happened. On those two days the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white clothes, and every dress was borrowed. Even the king's daughter borrowed from the high priest's daughter, and the high priest's daughter from the next family down, so that no girl who didn't own a fine dress would be put to shame. Nobody could tell whose family was rich. And they went out and danced in the vineyards, calling to the young men: lift your eyes and see whom you choose. The Mishnah doesn't say why either day was so happy. The Talmud fills that in later. Yom Kippur is easy: it was the day of forgiveness. For Tu B'Av, it collects several reasons. On this day, it says, the tribes were first allowed to marry one another. On this day the tribe of Benjamin, cut off after a terrible civil war in the book of Judges, was let back in. On this day, some say, the generation dying in the wilderness stopped dying. On this day the cutting of wood for the altar ended for the year, as the summer sun weakened. Most of the reasons are about a door opening: between tribes, back into a family, out of a long sentence. The calendar doesn't explain itself, but it does put the two days side by side. First the floor, the candle and the cry of how. Then, six days later, white dresses and dancing. Mourning is real, and it's given its full day, and it's not allowed to be the last word on the season. In Israel today Tu B'Av has come back as a day of love: weddings, flowers, songs on the radio. After mourning, love.
screen: `TET AND VAV: FIFTEEN.` · `EVERY DRESS WAS BORROWED.` · `DANCING IN THE VINEYARDS.` · `A DOOR OPENS.` · then, large: `AFTER MOURNING, LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: celebrate someone you love. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring one person to mind, a partner, a friend, a child, a parent, someone who has stood by you in a hard stretch. Picture their face as clearly as you can. Then think of one thing about them you've never quite said out loud: something they do that makes your life lighter. Let it fill you up for a while. You don't have to send it yet. Just hold the person and the thing together, the way you'd hold a gift before giving it. The bell holds the time.
Tu B'Av. The fifteenth of Av: borrowed white dresses, dancing in the vineyards, and a day of love six days after mourning. Today's word.
Your line: after mourning, love. Today, say the thing out loud, or write it down and send it, to the person you held in mind. Day six hundred ninety-five.

696.title: Year two close: the whole Torah
696.hook: the whole Torah, the whole prayer book, the whole year, now known from the inside
696.carry: the torah, the prayer, the year
696.howItsDone: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed in the synagogue, the congregation, often standing, calls out "chazak, chazak, venitchazek" (be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened), and the reader repeats it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu B'Av, borrowed white dresses and dancing in the vineyards. Your line was after mourning, love. Did you tell someone what they mean to you? Today, the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

Five times a year, something happens in the synagogue that happens at no other moment. The reader comes to the last verse of one of the five books of the Torah. In many congregations everyone rises, and the whole room calls out together, three words: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened. Not well done. Not congratulations. Be strong. This year, that shout came four times: at the end of Exodus, of Leviticus, of Numbers, of Deuteronomy. Today we stand up one more time, at the end of the whole year.
screen: `THE LAST VERSE OF A BOOK.` → `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, VENITCHAZEK.` → `FOUR BOOKS THIS YEAR.`

segments.voice: Look back at the road. Year two began in the middle of the plagues and walked the people out of Egypt, through the sea, to Sinai, and into a tent of meeting built from everyone's gifts. Then Leviticus, the book of holiness, with its offerings and its sudden line in the old Jewish translation: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Then Numbers, forty years of wilderness, complaints and manna and a donkey that talked. Then Deuteronomy, Moses' long goodbye, ending on Mount Nebo with a land he could see and not enter, and a grave no one knows. And on Simchat Torah the scroll rolled straight back to the beginning. Then the prayer book, walked in order. Waking up and thanking God for the rooster's sense to tell day from night. The Shema, with a hand over the eyes. The Amidah, standing, feet together, three steps in. Shabbat, and the quiet personal prayers at the end. Then the year: the Days of Awe, the sukkah, the lights of winter, Purim's noise, the Passover table, forty-nine days of counting, Sinai as a wedding, Ruth choosing to stay, and this summer's walls, floor and vineyards. Put it together and you have three circles, each one turning. The Torah is read through every year and begins again the moment it ends. The prayers come back three times a day. The year comes back every year. None of them is ever finished; that's the point. So the words at the end of a book aren't you made it. They're be strong, and the plural is the key: let us be strengthened, together. A people that keeps reading the same scroll, saying the same prayers, keeping the same days, holds each other up by doing it. Tomorrow the story walks on past the Torah's last page.
screen: `EXODUS TO DEUTERONOMY.` · `THE PRAYER BOOK, PAGE BY PAGE.` · `THE YEAR, FEAST AND FAST.` · `THREE CIRCLES, NEVER FINISHED.` · then, large: `THE TORAH, THE PRAYER, THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one blessing you learned this year. Settle, and breathe. Let a few of this year's blessings pass in front of you. The morning one for the soul: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure. The one that thanks God for giving strength to the weary. Blessed is the one who spoke, and the world came to be. If you pray, choose one and say it now, in Hebrew or in English, slowly, meaning every word. If you don't pray, say quietly the one line from this year that stayed with you. Then sit with it while the bell holds the time.
Year two close. The whole Torah, the whole prayer book, the whole Jewish year, walked from the inside, and three circles that keep turning. Be strong. Today's word.
Your line: the torah, the prayer, the year. Today, tell one person something you learned this year, and let them strengthen you back. Day six hundred ninety-six.
